E1689.summary: The sharp, discriminating spirit of the working leaven, which enters the philosopher's Mercury and causes it to putrefy.
E1689.body: Atwood describes the sharp, discriminating spirit of the working leaven, which enters the philosopher's Mercury and makes it putrefy: “this acute discriminative sulfuric Spirit occasions a putrefaction of the philosopher’s Mercury” [III.1 ¶24].

E1690.summary: One of the three principles: the hidden active, luminous ferment or soul of the matter, bound and imprisoned until it is freed, purified and fixed as the seed of gold.
E1690.body:
**Atwood.** Sulphur is one of the three principles, with mercury and salt, into which the ethereal hypostasis separates: “the soul, the spirit, and the body principle; the paternal, maternal, and proceeding substance of life; sulfur, mercury, salt” [III.1 ¶53]. It is “The sulfur, which is the soul and golden ferment” [III.1 ¶53]. In the dissolution the oppressive will dislocates it and it floats on the ethereal waters, and “the blackness” comes “from the sulfur” [III.1 ¶61]. In Sendivogius's fable Sal mortally wounds Sulfur [III.1 ¶53]. It is the active principle inside the philosophic water, “its own good sulfur, or vital flame”, and tripling it is part of the operator's weights: “to double mercury and triple sulfur” [I.3 n5]. The adepts give the name to light: “light or sulfur, as they call it, is the true form or seed of gold” [I.3 n40]. In the Mysteries it is “the re-entering Light of Reason in the Mysteries, which is that Sulfur of adepts, causing all this manifold scenery in the disruption of life” [II.3 ¶30]. In Sol it is the inner principle, imprisoned until the mercurial Spirit releases it: “his sulphur is imprisoned, so that he is not aware of it, does not feel or know himself” [III.3 ¶30]. 'Foliated sulphur' [I.3 ¶34] is not explained.

**Appendix (Table Talk, later layer).** “The Sulphur, the pure light of life, is bound down in the inferior mineral region of life” and “Saturn (i.e., Will) has the Key to the prison where Sulphur lies bound” [APP ¶125]; it must be drawn forth and grafted into the medial region to grow. It is “the masculine ferment, the sulphur or divine ferment” [APP ¶182], doubly hidden, to be set free to perfect the passive matter; also “the sulphur (this third, this obscure, this radical life)”, which must return on its matrix [APP ¶183]. “by sulphurs I mean forms” [APP ¶87]; “the impure sulphurs (desires, phantasms)” are the mundane desires in the individual will, to be purified or extirpated [APP ¶94].

**Quoted voices.** Hermes: “the fatness of our earth is sulphur” [I.3 ¶20]; “this sulphur doth tinge and fix, and is the connection of the tinctures” [I.3 ¶21]; “For the unguents are called sulphurs” [I.3 ¶24]. Atwood's notes gloss this: “The occult luminous principle of vitalization he calls sulfur, auripigment, etc.” [I.3 n24]; “the philosophic sulfur, or Light” [I.3 n25]; of the adepts, “The purified sulfur, fixed and incombustible, is the generating seed of the universal nature” [I.3 n29]. The Benedictine Monk: “the incombustible sulphur that heats or thickens the coldness and crudities of the quicksilver” until they are one body; Boehme places it in the red fire-form, “which is red, and therein the virtue, viz., sulphur is” [III.3 ¶24]. Eudoxus: the First Key opens “the dark prisons in which the Sulphur is shut up” [IV.3 ¶3]; “the Fire and the Sulphur are hidden in the centre of the Earth” [IV.3 ¶7]; “the precious ferment, the sulphur, that balm of Nature, and wonderful unguent” [IV.3 ¶8]; per Geber, “a mixture of Argent vive and Sulphur, that is to say, of the volatile and the fixed” [IV.3 ¶9]; the body must be dissolved, being “the body in which the Sulphur which coagulates the Mercury is enclosed” [IV.3 ¶12]; the true Mercury yields “the fixed Sulphur and the Universal Medicine” [IV.3 ¶16]. The Adept: Argent vive is defiled “being mingled with extraneous Sulfurs” but “coagulated by its own internal sulfur, red and white” [IV.1 ¶10]. Vaughan names “sulphurs simple and compounded” without explanation [IV.2 ¶35].

E1691.summary: A notion the quoted adept dismisses as one of the impostors' fables.
E1691.body: The adept quoted by Atwood rejects it: “those imposters who tell you of a sulphur tingens, and I know not what fables” [I.2 ¶8].

E1692.summary: In Ripley's Admonition, the 'Sun and Moon' of which our metals are said to be mines; not explained.
E1692.body: Ripley's Admonition, quoted by Atwood: “our mettalls be nought ells but miners too, Of our Soon and Moone” [II.1 ¶13]. The text does not explain the expression here.

E1693.summary: Named in a Sendivogius passage as the source of the 'beams' whose centres the lodestone's point answers; not explained.
E1693.body: In a passage of Sendivogius, a parenthetical gloss (speaker unclear) names the beams' source: “viz. of the sun and moon philosophical” [II.1 ¶10]. Not further explained.

E1694.summary: The higher work, served by the same bodily members as the natural work, in which a hyperphysical exudation supersedes natural secretion.
E1694.body: Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood: “All members that work here for the natural work, work also for the super-essential.” [APP ¶109] Its hyperphysical exudation supersedes natural secretion.

E1695.summary: Something not to be broken, according to a Pythagoric precept cited as a warning; not explained.
E1695.body: Cited as a warning: “Neither break a superficies, as the Pythagoric precept runs” [IV.3 ¶56]. Its meaning is not explained.

E1696.summary: In Psellus, the first kind of apparition in the Chaldaic rites, a mere appearance seen by the celebrant and not to be heeded; also a seeing in Hades.
E1696.body: Psellus, quoted by Atwood, names two kinds of apparition in the Chaldaic rites, “the first called superinspection, when he who celebrates the divine rites sees a mere apparition” such as light in some form; it is not to be heeded [II.3 ¶20]. Elsewhere he distinguishes “the Superinspection which takes place in Hades” from the Introspection [II.3 ¶46]; not further explained.

E1697.summary: Glossed as the Ideas of the Divine Mind, from which things generated below are infused as light.
E1697.body: Atwood's bracketed gloss: “the superior stars [i.e., Ideae Divinae Mentis]” [III.2 ¶19] (ours: Ideas of the Divine Mind). Things generated below are infused from them as light.

E1698.summary: In Vaughan, the higher and lower orders: superiors dissolve and inferiors coagulate; communion with superiors requires a heavenly life.
E1698.body: Vaughan, quoted by Atwood: “so superiors dissolve and inferiors coagulate” [III.4 ¶44]; without a heavenly life there is “no communion with superiors” [III.4 ¶44].

E1699.summary: The union in which no faculty of the soul is rejected, all being present under their rightful rule.
E1699.body: Atwood answers an objection: “Neither, we reply, is any faculty of the soul repudiated in that supernal alliance” [IV.4 ¶20]; all faculties are present under their rightful rule.

E1700.summary: The attraction by which the perfected Spirit draws the Homogeneal Nature into itself.
E1700.body: Atwood: the perfected Spirit draws the Homogeneal Nature into itself “by a supernatural magnetism” [IV.3 ¶29].

E1701.summary: In Eirenaeus, a later work whose commencement he sets apart from the literal labour on things as first found.
E1701.body: Eirenaeus, quoted by Atwood: “I am not speaking here indeed of the commencement of the Supernatural Work, but of things as we first find them” [IV.1 ¶6].

E1702.summary: Used of the latent nature of things implied by intellectual necessity, first in thought though later in time, and of the Kabalists' Law of Light; not defined.
E1702.body: Atwood speaks of “a superstantial nature of things implied which, though now latent and succeeding in order of time, is first in thought absolutely” [II.1 ¶34], and of the Kabalists' “an emanation of the great superstantial Law of Light” [II.1 ¶40]. The word itself is not defined.

E1703.summary: The deep experience of things reached by ascending in thought and then descending.
E1703.body: Atwood: by ascending in thought and then descending, one may “hope to penetrate so far as to the superstantial experience of things” [II.1 ¶49].

E1704.summary: Named in an objection asking why partaking things do not enjoy its light if true Being is everywhere present; not defined.
E1704.body: Named in an objection Atwood reports: if true Being is everywhere present, why do partaking things not enjoy “the light of the so-called superstantial world” [II.2 ¶20]? Not defined.

E1705.summary: In Plutarch, the object of the aspirant's knowledge, which the Goddess urges men to seek, dwelling in Reason as in a temple.
E1705.body: Plutarch, quoted by Atwood: the aim is “the attainment of the knowledge of the Supreme Mind, whom the Goddess exhorts them to search after” [II.1 ¶50]; it dwells in Reason as in a temple.

E1706.summary: Named for comparison: Engelbrecht lived, like him, in the visionary sphere.
E1706.body: Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): Atwood compares Engelbrecht to Swedenborg as living in the visionary sphere [APP ¶105].

E1707.summary: Cited for the idea of “correspondence” between the brain and the spiritual head.
E1707.body: Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): Atwood refers to the Swedenborgians' “correspondence” to illustrate the relation between brain and spiritual head [APP ¶15].

E1708.summary: The Sybil of Virgil's Aeneid, cited as drawing inspiration from supernal light and as directing Aeneas to the Golden Bough, which Atwood reads as the alchemical Gold.
E1708.body: Atwood cites the Sybil as drawing inspiration from rivers of supernal light [II.4 ¶13], and as enjoining peculiar rites and sacrifices to Misenus' remains, compared with those at Patroclus' pile [III.1 ¶25]. From Aeneid lib. 6 she quotes the Sybil's instruction on the Golden Bough, “Alte vestiga oculis: et rite repertum” [III.1 ¶15, III.1 ¶16, III.1 n17] (ours: search on high with the eyes, and when duly found…): it is sought by looking upward and yields only to one whom the fates call. Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): the Gold Alchemical is the gold Aeneas was told by the Sybil to find and gather [APP ¶20].

E1709.summary: A Sybil figure in Boissard cited for the recreation as a birth of the invisible into the palpable.
E1709.body: Atwood cites the Sybil in Boissard in support of the recreation as the birth of the invisible into the palpable: “Verbum invisible fiet palpabile et germinabit ut Radix.” [III.3 ¶79] (ours: The invisible Word will become palpable and will sprout as a Root).

E1710.summary: In Atwood's special sense, the true object of philosophy, implicating every science, sought through the categories as a channel for the Divine Intellect's birth into manifestation.
E1710.body: Atwood uses the word in a special sense: “That was the syllogism so important to be sought after, which also is according to Aristotle the true object of philosophy” [III.2 ¶42]. It implicates every science and is sought through the categories as a channel for the birth of the Divine Intellect into manifestation.

E1712.summary: Bishop-adept and Greek authority whom Atwood cites often and approvingly on the Matter, the phantastic Spirit, the two pairs of eyes, and the practical work.
E1712.body:
Atwood names Synesius among authors of extant treatises on the stone (with Heliodorus, Olympiodorus, Athenagoras, Zosimus, Archelaus) [I.1 ¶27, I.1 n34], cites his commentary on Democritus for the work's standing [I.1 ¶12, I.1 n15], and gives him as a bishop-adept who guarded the mysteries and bound initiation by oath [I.1 ¶27, I.1 n35, I.1 n36]. He is a Church Father adopting the Mysteries' rites, and among the Neoplatonists whose writings show the nature of the Mysteries, the disease of the Spirit and its clarification [II.2 ¶3, II.2 ¶9].

On the phantastic Spirit: “This Etherial Spirit, he says, is situated on the confines of the rational and brutal life” [II.2 ¶10]; he treats desire, will and assent, the purification of the imaginative soul and the trials of Hercules. Atwood endorses this as 'beautifully suggestive', an account of 'the life that is operated upon' and 'the artifice' [II.2 ¶13, II.2 ¶14, II.2 n11]. From de Somniis: “Intellect above all things separates whatever is contrary to the true purity of phantastic Spirit” [III.1 ¶20, III.1 n19]; demons are progeny of matter at war with the soul [II.3 ¶24, II.3 n26]. He names the defiled soul “Our viscous soul” [II.3 ¶30]. On Providence: efficacy of Divine Works [II.1 ¶52]; the two pairs of eyes, “this is an enigma indicative of contemplation and action” [III.1 ¶45, III.1 n49]; Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): “there are two pairs of eyes; those which are beneath are closed, when those which are above are opened” [APP ¶163].

On the Matter: his treatise closes the verbal instructions with “a clear Light, which fills with true virtue every mind that has once perceived it” [I.2 ¶33, I.2 n36]; 'the Greek saint' gives the summary, which Atwood calls plain words: “the Quintessence and hidden thing of our Stone is nothing else than our viscous celestial and glorious soul” [III.1 ¶70, III.1 ¶71]; he agrees with others concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60]. His True Book gives practical instruction on the one Water, which Atwood calls the Experiment of the Fathers: “labour only for that Water which burns to blackness, dissolves and congeals” [III.3 ¶60, III.3 n43].

E1713.summary: In Iamblichus, the theurgic aids and media which act of themselves toward divine union and properly excite the Divine will.
E1713.body: Iamblichus, quoted by Atwood: “the Synthemata, i.e., the Theurgic aids and media themselves” act of themselves toward divine union, “the things which properly excite the Divine will being the Divine Synthemata themselves” [II.4 ¶31].

E1714.summary: With Iris, the appearance of all colours after the darkness; a token of reconciliation.
E1714.body: Atwood: after the darkness “all the colours of the world will be apparent; also Iris, God’s messenger, and the tail of the peacock” [III.3 ¶13], a token of reconciliation.

E1715.summary: In Van helmont, that whose 'bars and bolts' a specific virtue looses.
E1715.body: Van helmont, quoted by Atwood, speaks of “a virtue of loosing the bars and bolts of Tartar” [IV.1 ¶39]. Not further explained.

E1716.summary: The region beyond Hades to which initiates were passed, the immortal abode; also called the death of this life and the Being of the central earth.
E1716.body: Atwood: Tartarus is the region beyond Hades to which the Hierophant passed initiates, “to its immortal abode: for such was Tartarus, the next beyond Hades” [II.3 ¶36]; she speaks of “the physical revealments of these Tartarean realms” [II.3 ¶34], and of the central earth, “but its Being is Tartarus” [II.3 ¶41]. Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): “Tartarus is the death of this life.” [APP ¶168], passed through by propitiation with the Golden Bough. Olympiodorus, reading Plato's Phaedo, gives it ethically as the place of the soul's trial and “physically, in that it is the wholeness of existence” [III.2 ¶9].

E1717.summary: Translator and commentator whose works Atwood uses as sources and praises as most erudite, while faulting his reading of the Mysteries as merely immaterial ceremonies.
E1717.body: Atwood relies on Taylor's translations and notes: his rendering of the Asclepian Dialogue and notes in Plotinus' Select Works [I.1 n11, I.1 n12]; his Pausanius notes for the Olympiodorus extract and for Porphyry [II.4 n1, II.4 n6]; Proculus on Euclid and a note to Aristotle's Metaphysics for the Synesius extract and the Anaxagoras passage [III.1 ¶21, III.1 n19]. She praises his Dissertation for setting forth Virgil's Elysian particulars [II.4 ¶16] and for showing the whole Odyssey to be an allegory of the recondite Wisdom of antiquity [IV.1 ¶22], and calls him the 'most erudite translator' who showed Aristotle's strictures misunderstood [III.2 ¶40, III.2 n36, III.2 n38]. She qualifies his Dissertation on the Eleusinian and Bacchic Mysteries: he examined them philosophically but still treated the rites as immaterial ceremonies representing abstract truths [II.2 ¶4, II.2 n5, II.2 n7].

E1718.summary: The blessed Water that nature sheds for the world, contemplated in the vestibule of the first Adytum.
E1718.body: Atwood: in the vestibule of the first Adytum one contemplates “the Tears of Isis, even that blessed Water which nature sheds divinely for the world” [III.3 ¶3].

E1719.summary: An adjective applied to Hercules' arcane labours and to the accomplishments by which initiates' souls are perfected; not defined.
E1719.body: Used (speaker unclear) of Hercules: “a part also of the regard of his arcane and telestic labours” [II.4 ¶3]. Atwood uses it of the Initiated, “being made perfect in every telestic accomplishment and virtue” [II.4 ¶39]. The word is not defined.
